channel.title: Simulatio Lab | New experiments
channel.description: New experiments from the lab that reruns the world

item.title: Why Can a Market Drop 7% in a Day? When Selling Triggers Selling
item.description: A 2% dip at the open, nearly 9% by the close. Watch "sell if it falls this far" lines topple one after another in an imaginary market, as a 3D wall of pillars.

item.title: If AI Takes the Junior Work, Where Will Tomorrow's Experts Come From?
item.description: Handing junior work to AI saves money now, but experts grow out of juniors. Watch, in 3D, the gap in an imaginary industry's ladder reach the upper floors.

item.title: When One Strait Is Blocked, Why Do Prices Rise in Faraway Countries?
item.description: Block one narrow strait on an imaginary globe. The rerouted cargo clogs other routes too, and prices rise in faraway countries.

item.title: Do Sanctions Break a Country, or Pull It Together?
item.description: With few joiners, goods slip back in; with many, people first close ranks. Run it on a trade web of 30 imaginary countries.

item.title: Close a Border Crossing, and Where Does the Flow Go?
item.description: Close one route and people spill onto the next, riskier ones. On an imaginary land, compare closing a route with easing the pressure to leave.

item.title: They Build Up, So We Build Up: Where Does an Arms Race Stop?
item.description: Two made-up countries that keep matching each other. Change reactions, burden, grievance and deals, and watch in 3D whether the arms towers settle or run away.

item.title: A Rising Power and a Leading One: Why Is It Dangerous When They Draw Even?
item.description: Run two made-up states for 100 years in 100 worlds and see in 3D how the risk of conflict peaks while one catches up.

item.title: Can You Ever Negotiate Again With a Country That Broke Its Word?
item.description: How long one betrayal lasts depends on how fast word spreads and how fast it fades. Run a 3D reputation network of 24 imaginary countries.

item.title: When the Algorithm Shows Only What You Like, Why Do Opinions Split?
item.description: An imaginary town's opinions start in the middle, then split into peaks at both ends as the feed shows more look-alike posts. Run it on a 3D opinion landscape.

item.title: When One Village Empties, Why Do the Villages Next Door Follow?
item.description: When the young leave, facilities close, and then even the next village empties faster. Watch this spiral spread on an imaginary 3D map.

item.title: With No Leader, How Does a Flock Fly as One?
item.description: Each bird watches only a few neighbors and follows three rules, yet thousands bend as one mass. Switch rules off and send a hawk in a 3D daytime sky.

item.title: Why Do Three Stars Dance So Unpredictably?
item.description: Run twin night skies where one star starts just 1% off. Two stars keep the same path to the end; when do three stars split apart? Time it yourself in 3D.

item.title: Nudge an Asteroid Years Ahead, and Will It Miss Earth?
item.description: When, and how hard, must you push an imaginary asteroid heading for Earth? Compare a gentle nudge ten years ahead with a hard shove a month ahead, in 3D.

item.title: When Two Galaxies Collide, Do Their Stars Crash?
item.description: Crash two 6,000-star galaxies in 3D. Stars barely brush past each other, yet the galaxies trail long tails and merge. Change the spin direction and how close they pass.

item.title: How Does Almost Even Dust Turn into a Web?
item.description: Switch on gravity for 32,768 grains only 2% uneven and they split into voids, threads and knots. Change the unevenness and expansion in a 3D box.

item.title: Why Haven't We Met an Alien Civilization Yet?
item.description: Roll seven numbers nobody knows as ranges 10,000 times, and watch civilizations light up, fade and send spreading signals in a 3D model galaxy.

item.title: Without the Moon, What Would Earth's Seasons Be Like?
item.description: The other planets keep nudging Earth's spin axis. Change the Moon's mass and watch in 3D how much the axis wobbles over a million years.

item.title: Why Are There Only a Few Bright Stars in the Night Sky?
item.description: Scatter 100,000 make-believe stars evenly and darken the sky: bright stars are a handful, while fainter ones grow about fourfold per step. Try city lights too.

item.title: Why Doesn't the Air Change When You Open Just One Window?
item.description: Two identical windows on opposite walls let wind sweep the room; on the same wall the air just swirls by the windows. Try it in a room seen from above.

item.title: When Two Countries Trade Tariff Blows, Why Do Both Lose?
item.description: Raising alone pays, but trading blows makes both lose. Watch two imaginary countries swap tariffs.

item.title: Same 48 Songs: Would Another World Crown Another Hit?
item.description: Release the same songs in 8 worlds that know nothing of each other. If people choose from the chart, does each world crown a different hit?

item.title: Why Do Some Pairs of Notes Sound Smooth and Others Grate?
item.description: Raise a second note slowly and measure how much the hidden overtones clash: calm valleys appear at spots like C–G. Listen and check for yourself.

item.title: If You Fling Paint at Random, Do You Get a Pollock?
item.description: A brush wanders at random flinging paint, and boxes are counted to measure how complex the picture is. Compare it with ruled straight lines for a surprise.

item.title: When One Person Stands, Why Does Everyone Stand?
item.description: When the same few stand first, the whole audience follows if they sit in front, and almost nobody if they sit in the back. Why?

item.title: How Many Dots Before a Face Starts to Appear?
item.description: Drop dots one by one where it is dark. First a smudge, then suddenly a face. How many does it take?

item.title: Why Does Even a Favorite Song Get Old by the 100th Listen?
item.description: A song that grew on you gets old one day. Compare simple and complex songs, heard daily or now and then.

item.title: Why Is One Shared Checkout Line Faster?
item.description: Same cashiers, same customers, different lines. Send the same shoppers to two stores and see who waits longer.

item.title: Why Do Buses Always Come in Pairs?
item.description: Evenly spaced buses end up travelling in bunches. Is it the drivers? Run a simple rule where more passengers means a longer stop.

item.title: How Many Strangers Can Fit on a Bench?
item.description: Everyone sat politely apart, yet seats go unused. Compare four ways of sitting side by side to see why.

item.title: Why Does My Bond Fall When Rates Rise?
item.description: New bonds pay more when rates rise, so why does the one I already bought lose value? Shake the rates and see for yourself.

item.title: Buying a High-Interest Currency: Up the Stairs, Down the Elevator
item.description: Buying a high-interest currency looks like easy money. But what happens when everyone piles in?

item.title: If Everyone Sends One More Class, Why Does No One Get Ahead?
item.description: If the family next door adds a class, should we? See how rank changes when one family sends more, and when everyone does.

item.title: Why Do Kids Keep Getting Sick at Daycare? Class Size and Staying Home
item.description: In a class of 20, how often does a cold go around in a year? See how class size and staying home when sick change the result.

item.title: Does Honesty Pay?
item.description: Four ways to place children in daycares. Does it pay to list your wishes in a different order than you really want?

item.title: How Many Should You Meet Before Choosing? The 37% Rule
item.description: If you can never go back to someone you passed, how many should you watch before choosing? Run it and find out.

item.title: Why Do Job Tips Come from Acquaintances?
item.description: Add just a few acquaintances to tight friend circles, and news spreads at a very different speed. Try it yourself.

item.title: Nobody Wants It, So Why Does War Happen?
item.description: War costs both sides. So why does it happen? Run broken talks, arms races and spreading to neighbors.

item.title: How Did Farming Cross a Continent?
item.description: With just two rules, people multiply and spread to neighbors, farming creeps across a continent about 1 km a year. Really?

item.title: Why Double the Soldiers Is Four Times as Strong
item.description: Blue and red armies wear each other down. Why does twice the soldiers mean four times the strength? Try splitting an army in two.

item.title: Why Do Lightning, Coral and Snowflakes Look Alike?
item.description: A wandering particle sticks when it touches. That is the only rule, yet branches grow by themselves. Want to grow one?

item.title: Can a Single Grain of Sand Cause an Avalanche?
item.description: Pile sand one grain at a time and the heap ends up on the edge of collapse. The same grain sometimes does nothing, sometimes starts an avalanche.

item.title: Why Does Putting Out Every Small Fire Lead to Bigger Ones?
item.description: A forest where every small fire is put out can burn in one huge blaze later. Compare it with a forest left alone.

item.title: A Two-Rule Ant Suddenly Builds a Road
item.description: An ant with just two rules wanders messily for a long time, then suddenly starts building a straight road. Nobody planned it, so why?

item.title: Why Do My Friends Have More Friends Than I Do?
item.description: Is it because you are unpopular? Build a network and click a person to see why almost everyone feels this way.

item.title: A New Road Made Everyone Slower
item.description: We opened one more shortcut in a jammed city. Everyone picked their fastest route. So what happens to the commute?

item.title: Praise Them and They Slip, Scold Them and They Improve
item.description: Even if words do nothing, the best do worse next time and the worst do better. Why?

item.title: Bullet Holes on the Planes That Came Back: Where Should the Armor Go?
item.description: Returned planes have the most holes in the wings and fuselage. Is that where the armor should go?

item.title: Why Does the Bus Always Make You Wait Longer?
item.description: The bus comes every 10 minutes on average, so why do you always wait longer? We also check why your class always feels crowded.

item.title: A Coincidence That Isn't a Coincidence?
item.description: Meeting someone with your birthday feels spooky. But is it really so rare? Change the headcount and find out for yourself.

item.title: Phantom Traffic Jams: Why Does Traffic Stop Without an Accident?
item.description: Cars suddenly stop with no accident or roadwork. Can a jam appear even when everyone follows the rules?

item.title: Why Is the Popular Restaurant Always Packed?
item.description: Why does everyone lose when everyone thinks alike? Change how people predict and run it yourself.

item.title: What Happens When Queue-Jumping Spreads?
item.description: If cutting pays and scolding costs, does the line fall apart? Change the strength of scolding and see.

item.title: Why Birds of a Feather Flock Together
item.description: "Diverse neighbors are fine, I just want a third to be like me." What happens to a neighborhood of such easygoing people?

item.title: How Does a Rumor Spread in Group Chats?
item.description: One rumor in a group chat soon becomes something everyone knows. How late can a correction come and still matter?

item.title: Does Lowering Your Standards Help You Find a Match?
item.description: If everyone wants someone better than themselves, when do matches happen? Change how high people aim and watch the search time.

item.title: Is Success Effort or Luck?
item.description: Effort is similar across people, so why does wealth pile up in a few hands? Rerun 1,000 people's 40 years yourself.

item.title: Why Does Money Pile Up Even in Fair Bets?
item.description: Everyone starts equal and only makes fair coin-flip bets. Does money still pile up in a few hands? How much sharing stops it?

item.title: Why Do Only the Top 1% of YouTubers Break Through?
item.description: Do good videos win, or do channels that broke out first keep winning? Run a subscriber race of 200 channels yourself.

item.title: Why Does Winning an Auction Cost You?
item.description: The highest bidder wins, so why do winners lose money on average? Change the number of bidders and see for yourself.

item.title: How Do Apartment Prices Spread?
item.description: Does a price rise in one neighborhood spread to the next ones? Change how much they copy neighbors, the loan cap and a rate shock, and watch.

item.title: Why Do Incompetent Bosses Exist?
item.description: Does promoting your best performer make a company better? Compare promotion methods in a 160-person company.

item.title: If Korea's Births Stay This Low, What Will 2070 Look Like?
item.description: Change births, migration and how long people live, and watch Korea's population by age change year by year to 2070.

item.title: Does the Voting Method Change the Winner?
item.description: If the same people vote with the same preferences, can the way votes are counted change the winner? Compare four methods.

item.title: How Does a Revolution Begin?
item.description: What if everyone decides by watching how many others came out? Watch a few sparks fill the whole square.

item.title: Why Did Easter Island Collapse?
item.description: The forest feeds the people and the people cut the forest. Can that alone make a population boom and then shrink? Run it and see.

item.title: How Does a Single Shot Become a World War?
item.description: How far does a small clash spread? Change how tight the alliances are and how well pacts are kept, and run it yourself.

item.title: Why Do Fireflies Flash in Unison?
item.description: Nobody conducts them, yet hundreds flash together. Can just seeing each other's light line them up?

item.title: How Does a Zebra Get Its Stripes?
item.description: Nobody draws them, yet spots and stripes appear on their own. Change just two numbers and see which pattern grows.

item.title: Do Nice People Survive?
item.description: Do people who trust and cooperate just get betrayed? Run a village where half are cheaters and see if cooperation spreads or collapses.

item.title: If You Did Not Know Who You Would Be Born As, Which Society Would You Pick?
item.description: If you had to pick a society without knowing if you'd be rich or poor, which one? See how the answer changes with how much you dislike risk.

item.title: Is the Tragedy of the Commons Inevitable?
item.description: Does a fishery everyone shares always run dry? Try it with and without watching and fines.

item.title: Can Monkeys Write Hamlet?
item.description: Could monkeys typing at random write a line of Hamlet? Race hitting it in one go against building it up step by step.

item.title: Why Are a Few Words Used Constantly?
item.description: In any text, a few words make up most of it. Could simply copying earlier words cause that?

item.title: How Do Stories Change as They're Retold?
item.description: What survives and what disappears when a story is passed on 40 times? Change memory and embellishment and see.

item.title: Why Does Fashion Go in Cycles?
item.description: What happens when some people copy others and some run away to look different? Adjust both forces and watch whether fashion keeps cycling.

item.title: What If 100 AI Painters Copy Each Other?
item.description: If painters keep copying each other, do their pictures start to look the same? Change how much they copy and see.

item.title: Why Do Sunflower Seeds Sit at That Exact Angle?
item.description: Change the angle you turn as each seed is placed. Which angle fills the disc evenly with no gaps?
